lessons.title: Booking a table
lessons.goal: Reserve a table by phone for a day, time and group size.

tip.title: Quería: the polite way to ask
tip.body: Use quería (literally "I wanted") to make a polite request: Quería reservar una mesa. Quisiera works too and is even more formal. The restaurant will ask ¿Para cuántas personas? and ¿A nombre de quién?, and you give the group size with somos: Somos cuatro. In Spain you make una reserva; in Mexico people usually say una reservación.

lessons.title: Ordering a full meal
lessons.goal: Order a starter, main course, dessert and drink.

tip.title: De primero, de segundo, de postre
tip.body: A full meal in Spain comes in courses: de primero (first course), de segundo (main course) and de postre (dessert). Order each one with de …: De primero, la sopa. The waiter asks ¿Qué van a tomar? (tomar is used for food and drink) and ¿Y para beber?. If you want the same as someone else, say Para mí, lo mismo. In Mexico you'll also hear ordenar for "to order"; pedir works everywhere.

phrases.n: Do you know what you'd like?
phrases.note: Said to a group. To one person: ¿Ya sabe qué va a tomar?

phrases.n: What does the set menu include?

phrases.t: De primero, la sopa de verduras.

lessons.title: Allergies & special requests
lessons.goal: Ask what's in a dish and explain what you can't eat.

tip.title: ¿Qué lleva?
tip.body: To ask what's in a dish, use llevar: ¿Qué lleva? ¿Lleva gluten? For allergies, Tengo alergia a … works for everyone; Soy alérgico (man) / alérgica (woman) a … is also common. Sin means without: sin queso, sin cebolla. Some foods change name: peanuts are cacahuetes in Spain and cacahuates in Mexico. In Mexico, picar means "to be spicy": always worth asking ¿Pica mucho?

phrases.t: Tengo alergia a los frutos secos.

phrases.n: Does it have onion in it?
Do you have any vegetarian dishes?
Can you make it for me without cheese?
phrases.note: lo = el plato. More on this in lesson 4.

lines.n: They're a little spicy, but I can bring you the sauce on the side.

lines.t: Perfecto. ¿Y me las puede preparar sin cebolla?

lessons.title: lo, la, me, le: object pronouns
lessons.goal: Say "it", "to me" and "to you" without repeating the noun.

tip.title: ¿Me lo trae?
tip.body: Pronouns save you repeating the noun. The thing you order becomes lo, la, los or las, matching its gender and number: ¿El vino? Lo pido yo. ¿La sopa? La quiero sin sal. The person who receives something is me (to me), te (to you) or le (to him, her or usted): ¿Me trae la carta? Le recomiendo el pescado. Pronouns go before the conjugated verb. With two pronouns, the person comes first: ¿Me lo trae? (Can you bring it to me?). Le + lo/la would sound awkward, so le changes to se: Se lo traigo (I'll bring it to you).

story.title: A small problem
story.intro: Lucía and Andrés are having dinner at a restaurant in Mexico City, but not everything goes to plan.

lines.name: Lucía
lines.t: Andrés, ¿ya probaste la sopa? Está fría, ¿no?
lines.n: Andrés, have you tried the soup? It's cold, isn't it?

lines.name: Andrés
lines.t: Sí, está fría. Y además yo pedí tacos de pescado, no de pollo.
lines.n: Yes, it's cold. And also I ordered fish tacos, not chicken.

lines.name: Lucía
lines.t: ¡Disculpe! Esto no es lo que pedimos.
lines.n: Excuse me! This isn't what we ordered.

lines.name: Mesera
lines.t: ¿Qué pasó? ¿Hay algún problema?
lines.n: What happened? Is there a problem?

lines.name: Andrés
lines.t: La sopa está fría y mi plato no es el correcto. Pedí tacos de pescado.
lines.n: The soup is cold and my dish isn't the right one. I ordered fish tacos.

lines.name: Mesera
lines.t: Tiene razón, disculpe las molestias. Ahora mismo les traigo otra sopa y se los cambio.
lines.n: You're right, sorry for the inconvenience. I'll bring you another soup right away and change them for you.

lines.name: Mesera
lines.t: Aquí tienen. Y el postre va por cuenta de la casa.
lines.n: Here you are. And the dessert is on the house.

lines.name: Lucía
lines.t: ¡Qué amable! Muchas gracias.
lines.n: How kind! Thank you very much.

culture.title: Menú del día, comida corrida and tipping
culture.body: On weekdays many restaurants in Spain offer a menú del día at lunchtime: a fixed price for a first course, a main course, dessert or coffee, bread and a drink. In Mexico the equivalent is the comida corrida, a set lunch that often starts with soup and rice before the main dish, usually with tortillas and an agua fresca. Tipping customs differ: in Spain a tip is optional and usually small, and many people just round up or leave a few coins. In Mexico a tip (la propina) of around 10–15% is customary in sit-down restaurants.
